The story makes extensive use of subtext, which naturally enriches both the characterization and the contrasting settings of the working-class supermarket and Miss Emily's upper-class world, rather than feeling forced. 

For example, when Nell visits Miss Emily's house for the first time, the surface-level description notes that "A woman named June brought us tea and did not meet my eyes" and that Nell sat in "a chair that was worth more than my rent." The subtext here effortlessly establishes the rigid class hierarchy of the setting and Nell's acute discomfort in crossing from the working-class side of that divide to the wealthy side. Similarly, when Miss Emily calls Nell and Graham's rented apartment "charming," the subtext—which Nell explicitly learns to decode as meaning "a place where things break"—reveals Miss Emily's quiet disdain for their modest lifestyle and the subtle, ongoing pressure she exerts to assimilate Nell into her sphere of wealth and control. Finally, Nell's return to the Foodfair and her attachment to her name tag carry the subtext of a woman fighting to preserve her identity and autonomy against the overwhelming, albeit well-intentioned, influence of her mother-in-law's world.
